'''''Iris sanguinea''''' is a [[rhizome|rhizomatous]] flowering plant in the [[genus]] ''[[Iris (plant)|Iris]]'' and in the series ''[[Iris ser. Sibiricae|Sibiricae]]''. It is cultivated as an ornamental plant in [[temperateness|temperate]] regions. It is one of the species considered a [[Japanese iris]]. It is from [[Asia]], found between Russia, [[Mongolia]], [[China]],  [[Japan]]  and [[Korea]]. It has grey green leaves, an unbranched flowering stem and flowers in reddish-purple shades, from blue to blue-purple, red-violet, with a rare white variant.

A 2020 taxonomic revision suggests that previously distinguished taxa of ''Iris sanguinea'' and ''[[Iris sibirica]]'' bear no [[Phylogenetics|phylogenetic]] nor [[Morphology (biology)|morphological]] distinction. As such, name ''I. sanguinea'' was synonymized with ''I. siberica''.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Boltenkov |first1=Eugeny |last2=Artyukova |first2=Elena |last3=Kozyrenko |first3=Marina |last4=Erst |first4=Andrey |last5=Trias-Blasi |first5=Anna |date=2020-10-01 |title=Iris sanguinea is conspecific with I. sibirica (Iridaceae) according to morphology and plastid DNA sequence data |journal=PeerJ |language=en |volume=8 |article-number=e10088 |doi=10.7717/peerj.10088 |issn=2167-8359 |pmc=7533061 |pmid=33062454 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Description==
It has a thick creeping rhizome.<ref name="FOC" />

It has grey-green leaves that are more or less the same height as the flowering stems,<!-- also <ref name=stebbings/> --><ref name=European/><ref name=ClaireAustin/><ref name=handbook>{{cite web| first=William | last=Dykes| title=Handbook of Garden Irises | year=2009| url=http://www.beardlessiris.org/reviews/handbook%20of%20garden%20irises%20-%20dykes.pdf |  publisher=beardlessiris.org (The Group for Beardless Irises) | access-date=1 November 2014}}</ref> but as the leaves droop, they appear shorter.<ref name=cassidy>{{cite book |last1=Cassidy |first1=George E.| last2=Linnegar | first2=Sidney | date=1987 |edition=Revised  | title= Growing Irises  |location=Bromley | publisher=Christopher Helm | page=132 | isbn=0-88192-089-4}}</ref><!-- also <ref name=bbc/> --> The linear, narrow leaves grow between 20 and 60 cm long and 5–13 mm wide.<ref name=FOC/><ref name=European/><!-- also <ref name=rhs/> -->

It has a hollow unbranched flowering stem, that grows up to between {{convert|30|and|90|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} long.<ref name="stebbings">{{cite book |last=Stebbings |first=Geoff |url=https://archive.org/details/gardenersguideto00steb |title=The Gardener's Guide to Growing Irises |publisher=David and Charles |year=1997 |isbn=0-7153-0539-5 |location=Newton Abbot |page=[https://archive.org/details/gardenersguideto00steb/page/45 45] |url-access=registration}}</ref><ref name=signa/><ref name=FOC/><!-- also <ref name=European/><ref name=ClaireAustin/><ref name=handbook/><ref name=cassidy/><ref name=bbc/><ref name=rhs/><ref name=america/><ref name=pacific/><ref name=daves/> -->
The stems bear two to three flowers,<!-- also <ref name=stebbings/> --><ref name=FOC/><ref name=cassidy/><ref name=rhs/> at the terminal ends in early summer,<ref name=European/><ref name=rhs/><ref name=daves/> between May and July.<ref name=signa/><ref name=FOC/><ref name=ClaireAustin/>

It has three green [[spathe]]s (leaves of the flower bud), that are reddish at the base, measuring 5–7 cm long and 1 cm wide.<ref name=FOC/><ref name=European/> It then has a brown papery tip.<ref name=European/>

The flowers come in a range of reddish-purple shades,<!-- also <ref name=European/> --><ref name=rhs/><ref name=america/><ref name=daves/> from blue to blue-purple, red-violet, with a rare white variants.<!-- also <ref name=signa/><ref name=FOC/><ref name=ClaireAustin/><ref name=handbook/><ref name=handbook/> --><ref name=cassidy/><ref name=pacific/><ref name=daves/> The flowers are 6–8 cm in diameter.<ref name=stebbings/><!-- also <ref name=FOC/> --><ref name=European/><ref name=rhs/>

It has two pairs of petals, three large [[sepals]] (outer petals), known as the 'falls' and three inner, smaller petals (or [[tepals]], known as the 'standards'). The large obovate (shaped like an egg), drooping 'falls' have reddish-purple veins on a white or yellowish signal.<!-- also <ref name=signa/><ref name=FOC/><ref name=European/><ref name=ClaireAustin/><ref name=handbook/> --><ref name=cassidy/><ref name=rhs/><ref name=pacific/>
The smaller, erect obovate standards are 4–5 cm long and 1.5 cm wide.<ref name=FOC/><ref name=European/><ref name=ClaireAustin/>

It has perianth tube of 8–10 mm long, 3 cm long white filaments, yellow anthers, a cylindric ovary 1.5–2 cm long by 3–4 mm wide, and a reddish-purple style branches 3.5 cm long by 5 mm wide.<ref name=FOC/>

In July and September (after the iris has flowered), it produces a seed capsule, which is ellipsoid or cylindric in form and measures 3.5–5 cm long by 1.2–1.5 cm wide.<ref name=FOC/><ref name=handbook/><ref name=cassidy/>

===Biochemistry===
In 2012, a genetic study was carried out on ''[[Iris laevigata]]'' and several of its closely related iris species, including ''[[Iris ensata]]'', ''[[Iris setosa]]'', ''[[Iris halophila]]'', ''[[Iris scariosa]]'', ''[[Iris potaninii]]'', ''[[Iris tenuifolia]]'', ''[[Iris bloudowii]]'', and ''Iris sanguinea''.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sun |first1=Ming-Zhou |last2=Li |first2=Ming-Rui |last3=Shi |first3=Feng-Xue |last4=Li |first4=Lin |last5=Liu |first5=Ying |last6=Li |first6=Lin-Feng |last7=Xiao |first7=Hong-Xing |date=July 2012 |title=Genomic and EST-derived microsatellite markers for Iris laevigata (Iridaceae) and other congeneric species |journal=American Journal of Botany |volume=99 |issue=7 |pages=286–288 |doi=10.3732/ajb.1100608 |pmid=22739712 |bibcode=2012AmJB...99.e286S }}</ref>

As most irises are [[diploid]], having two sets of [[chromosomes]], this can be used to identify hybrids and classification of groupings.<ref name=ClaireAustin>{{cite book | first= Claire | last=Austin | title= Irises: A Gardener's Encyclopedia | publisher= Timber Press, Incorporated | isbn = 978-0-88192-730-6 | year = 2005 | ol = OL8176432M | page=<!-- 274–275  in diff edition-->}}</ref>
It has been count various times; 2n=28, Simonet, 1928; 2n=26,28 Lee, 1970; 2n=28, Starodubtsev & Mironova, 1990; 2n=28, Huang, S.-f. & Zhao, 1995.<ref name=america/>
2n=28 is the most common listed count.<ref name=signa>{{cite web |first=D. |last=Kramb |title=Iris sanguinea |date=8 November 2003 |url=http://www.signa.org/index.pl?Iris-sanguinea |publisher=signa.org (Species Iris Group of North America) |access-date=27 December 2014}}</ref><ref name=pacific>{{cite web| title=Iris summary |date=14 April 2014 |url=http://www.pacificbulbsociety.org/pbswiki/files/Iris/Iris_Summary.pdf |publisher=pacificbulbsociety.org | access-date=23 November 2014}}</ref>
This means it is similar to ''[[Iris sibirica]]'' and ''[[Iris typhifolia]]''.<ref name=ClaireAustin/>

Specimens from [[Primorsky Krai|Primorskii Krai]] in Russia, were found to have a chromosome count of 2n=28.<ref name=iapt>{{cite web | editor=Karol Marhold | title=IAPT/IOPB chromosome data 14 | date=December 2012 | url=http://www.iopb.org/PDF/IAPT_IOPB_Chr_data14.pdf | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130605033132/http://www.iopb.org/PDF/IAPT_IOPB_Chr_data14.pdf | archive-date=June 5, 2013 | publisher=iopb.org | access-date=5 November 2014 }}</ref>

== Taxonomy==
[[File:Siberian Iris Iris siberica Flower Unopened 2000px.jpg|thumb|showing the red-purple colour of the spathes of the iris – giving it its name of blood iris (''Iris sanguinea'')]]
''Iris sanguinea'' is pronounced as ''EYE-ris san-GWIN-ee-a''.<ref name=daves>{{cite web |title=PlantFiles: Japanese Iris, Siberian Iris |url=http://davesgarden.com/guides/pf/go/80085/ |publisher=davesgarden.com |access-date=27 December 2014}}</ref>

It is written as 溪荪 in [[Chinese characters|Chinese script]] and known as ''xi sun'' in China.<ref name=FOC>{{cite web |title=FOC Vol. 24 Page 301 |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200028208 |publisher=efloras.org |website=Flora of China |access-date=27 December 2014}}</ref> In [[Japanese language|Japanese]] it is known as ''ayame'' and written as アヤメ, 菖蒲, 文目 in Japanese script.<ref>{{cite web |title=Iris (ayame) |date=19 September 2005 |url=http://worldkigodatabase.blogspot.co.uk/2005/09/iris-ayame.html |publisher=worldkigodatabase.blogspot.co.uk |access-date=2 January 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Ayame (Iris sanguinea) flowers in Tokei-ji |date=10 June 2012 |url=http://www.thegardenofzen.com/2012/06/ayame-iris-sanguinea-flowers-in-tokei.html |publisher=thegardenofzen.com |access-date=2 January 2015}}</ref>

It has the common names of ''blood-red iris''<ref name=rhs>{{cite web |title=Iris sanguinea |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/9352/Blood-red-iris/Details |publisher=rhs.org.uk |access-date=27 December 2014}}</ref><ref name=grin>{{GRIN | accessdate=27 December 2014}}</ref> and ''blood iris''.<ref name=botanical>{{cite web |first=Jennifer |last=McDonald |title=A non-bloody blood iris |url=http://botanicalmusings.blogspot.co.uk/2012/05/non-bloody-blood-iris.html |date=16 May 2012 |publisher=botanicalmusings.blogspot.co.uk |access-date=27 December 2014}}</ref><ref name=pfaf>{{cite web |title=Iris sanguinea |url=http://www.pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Iris+sanguinea |publisher=pfaf.org  |access-date=27 December 2014}}</ref>

It was originally published as ''Iris orientalis'' by [[Carl Peter Thunberg|Thunberg]] in ''Transactions of the Linnean Society'' Vol. 2 page 328 in 1794, but the name had already been used for an iris within the [[Iris series Spuriae|series Spuriae Iris]].<ref name=america>{{cite web |first=Terry |last=Laurin |title=(SPEC) Iris sanguinea Hornem ex Donn. Date=19 September 2014 |url=http://wiki.irises.org/bin/view/Spec/SpecSanguinea |publisher=wiki.irises.org (American Iris Society) |access-date=27 December 2014}}</ref>

It was first published as ''Iris sanguinea'', described by [[Jens Wilken Hornemann]] in ''Hortus Regius Botanicus Hafniensis'' (In Usum Tyronum et Botanophilorum. Hauniae) (Copenhagen) issue 58 in 1813.<ref>{{cite web |title=Iridaceae Iris sanguinea Hornem. Hornemann, Jens Wilken (1770–1841) |url=http://www.ipni.org/ipni/idPlantNameSearch.do?id=439065-1 |publisher=ipni.org ([[International Plant Names Index]]) |access-date=13 December 2014}}</ref> But this was based on an earlier description by [[James Donn]] in 'Hortus Cantabrigensis.' Vol. 6, 17 in 1811.<ref name=america/>

In 1981, in his book ''The Iris'', [[Brian Mathew]] uses the name ''Iris sanguinea'' Donn.<ref name=america/> This was then used by other authors.(See [[#Sources|Other Sources]] section)

The Latin [[Botanical name#Binary name|specific epithet]] ''sanguinea'' refers to the Latin word for blood, referring to the red-purple colour of the spathe valves of the iris.<ref name=dykesonirises>{{cite web| first=William | last=Dykes |title=Dykes on Iris| url=http://www.beardlessiris.org/reviews/dykes%20on%20irises%20-%20part1.pdf |publisher=beardlessiris.org (The Group for Beardless Irises) | access-date=21 November 2014}}</ref>

This plant has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref name=rhs/>

It was verified by [[United States Department of Agriculture]] [[Agricultural Research Service]] on 15 March 2002.<ref name=grin/>

In 2020, a [[Taxonomy (biology)|taxonomic]] revision of [[Iris ser. Sibiricae|''Iris'' ser. ''Sibiricae'']] showed no phylogenetic separation between ''[[Iris sibirica]]'', ''Iris sanguinea'', and ''[[Iris typhifolia]]''. Moreover, no morphological character was found to define clear boundaries between taxa. As such, ''I. sanguinea'' and ''I. typhifolia'' were synonymized with ''I. sibirica''.<ref name=":0" />

==Distribution and habitat==
''Iris sanguinea'' is native to the temperate regions of eastern [[Asia]].<ref name=grin/>

===Range===
It is found between Russia (East of [[Lake Baikal]] in [[Siberia]],<ref name=signa/><ref name=pacific/> [[Buryatia]], [[Chita Oblast|Chita]], [[Irkutsk Oblast|Irkutsk]], [[Amur Oblast|Amur]], [[Khabarovsk Krai|Khabarovsk]], [[Magadan Oblast|Magadan]] and [[Primorsky Krai|Primorye]]),<ref name=grin/> [[Mongolia]], [[China]] ([[Provinces of China|provinces]] of [[Heilongjiang]], [[Jiangsu]], [[Jilin]], [[Liaoning]] and [[Nei Monggol]]),<ref name=FOC/><ref name=grin/> [[Japan]] ([[Hokkaido]], [[Honshu]] and [[Shikoku]]) and [[Korea]].<!-- also <ref name=stebbings/><ref name=signa/><ref name=FOC/><ref name=European/><ref name=ClaireAustin/><ref name=cassidy/><ref name=america/> --><ref name=pacific/><ref name=grin/><ref name=botanical/>

===Habitat===
It grows in damp meadows,<ref name=signa/><ref name=FOC/><ref name=cassidy/> along the edges of rivers and lakes,<ref name=signa/><ref name=FOC/><ref name=ClaireAustin/> on the edges of forests,<ref name=signa/>  beside streams and on hillsides,<ref name=FOC/> at altitudes of around 500 metres above sea level.<ref name=FOC/>

==Cultivation==
''Iris sanguinea'' is thought to be easy to grow.<ref name=bbc>{{cite web |title=iris sanguinea |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/gardening/plants/plant_finder/plant_pages/12109.shtml |publisher=bbc.co.uk |access-date=27 December 2014}}</ref><ref name=botanical/> It is sometimes described as "prolific", meaning it can be invasive when the conditions are optimal.<ref name=botanical/>

It will tolerate temperatures of {{convert|-3.8|°C|°F|abbr=on}} down to {{convert|-34.4|°C|°F|abbr=on}}.<ref name=daves/> It is [[Hardiness (plants)|hardy]] to [[USDA]] Zone 4–9,<ref name=daves/> and Zone H2 (which means hardy to {{convert|-15|to|-20|C|F}}<ref>{{cite web|title=Plant Hardiness  |url=http://theseedsite.co.uk/hardiness.html |publisher=theseedsite.co.uk |access-date=20 December 2014}}</ref>), in Europe.<ref name=European>James Cullen, Sabina G. Knees, H. Suzanne Cubey (Editors) {{Google books|CkxWrDqtWLQC|The European Garden Flora Flowering Plants: A Manual for the Identification|page=252}}</ref> It is hardy in the UK,<ref name=bbc/><ref name=rhs/> but will not survive wet winters in cooler parts of the world.<ref name=ClaireAustin/>

The iris should be grown in well-drained,<ref name=bbc/><ref name=rhs/> neutral to slightly acidic soils (the [[pH level]] should be more than 5.6) with plenty of organic matter,<ref name=daves/><ref name=botanical/> or loam.<ref name=rhs/>

It prefers positions in full sun,<ref name=bbc/><ref name=daves/> but can tolerate partial shade (with some hours of sunlight).<ref name=rhs/>

The plant needs moisture during the growing season (in spring and early summer) to create the best blooms.<ref name=bbc/><ref name=daves/> But it does not grow in the water, although it will tolerate occasional flooding.<ref name=botanical/>

===Propagation===
They are best propagated by division.<ref name=daves/> The divisions must be not be allowed to dry out and can be temporarily stored in bucket of water, while the new planting position is prepared.<ref name=daves/> The best time to divide plants is between August and September.<ref name=bbc/><ref name=rhs/><ref name=pfaf/>

To grow from seed, allow the mature pods to dry on the plant. Then break open to collect seeds and the direct sow outdoors in fall or autumn.<ref name=rhs/><ref name=daves/><ref name=botanical/><ref name=pfaf/> The seed should germinate within three months, if they have been pre-chilled for four weeks or placed outdoors over winter. Once germinated they should be brought indoors (or place in a cold frame<ref name=pfaf/>) to avoid temperature shock and then transplant outside, when the plant has four leaves. The climatic conditions of the garden, controls planting (or transplanting) times. In the north, they are best planted in the spring (avoiding frost damage to tender roots).<ref name=pfaf/> In the south, they are best planted in the autumn (or fall), which avoids the hot dry period.<ref name=botanical/><ref name=pfaf/>

They can be used in gardens, at waterside locations beside pools, ponds or streams.<ref name=bbc/>

It is naturally propagated by pollinating insects such as bees which will feed on its nectar.<ref name=botanical/>

===Hybrids and cultivars===
Iris sanguinea has been hybridized with ''Iris sibirica'', to extend the blue colour range.<ref name=stebbings/><ref name=European/>

Iris sanguinea crosses:
* ''Iris sanguinea'' × ''Iris sibirica''; 'Abitibi'; 'Chaudiere'; 'Gatineau'; 'Kootenay'; 'Madawaska'; 'Matane'; 'Ottawa'; 'Pembina'; 'Pickaninny'; 'Pickanock'; 'Richelieu'; 'Soothsayer'; 'Rideau'; 'Rimouski'
* ''Iris sanguinea'' × ''[[Iris chrysographes]]'': 'Aegea';
* ''Iris sanguinea'' × ''[[Iris hookeri]]''; 'Humble Path';
* ''Iris sanguinea'' × ''[[Iris setosa]]''; 'Orientosa';
* ''Iris sanguinea'' ×  [[Iris ser. Californicae|Series Californiae]] (Cal-Sibes); 'Crimson Accent';
* ''Iris sanguinea'' × ''[[Iris ensata]]''; 'Adrenaline Rush';
* ''Iris sanguinea'' × ''[[Iris versicolor]]''; 'Lillabelle';<ref name=america/>
A known variant in Japan is ''Iris sanguniea var. violacea''. (Makino),<ref name=signa/><ref>{{cite web |title=Iris sanguinea var. violacea Makino is an accepted name |url=http://www.theplantlist.org/tpl1.1/record/kew-329471 |publisher=theplantlist.org |access-date=2 January 2015}}</ref> which has deep violet flowers with larger than normal standards.<ref name=European/>

It also has the following known cultivars;
'Annick'; 'Baby Sister'; 'Blue King'; 'Coreana'; 'Dreams'; 'Emperor'; 'Fairy Fingers'; 'Flossie Bobbsy'; 'Grace Ashley'; 'Haematophylla'; 'Kamayama';<ref>{{cite web |title=Iris |date=5 June 2010 |url=http://www.shieldsgardens.com/Blogs/Garden/201006.html |publisher=shieldsgardens.com |access-date=2 January 2015}}</ref>'Kobana'; 'La Blanchefleur'; 'Nana'; 'Nana Alba' (white flowers usually with some purple veins);<ref name=European/>  'Nertchinskia'; 'Orientalis Alba'.; Orientalis Alba Stellata'; 'Sanguinea 1615'; 'Sanguinea 1616'; 'Snowcrest'; 'Snow Queen';<ref name=bbc/> 'Sorak Blue'; 'Tetrapetala'; 'Trigonocarpa'; 'Yankee Trader'; 'Yixingensis';<ref name=america/>

==Toxicity==
As in many other irises, most parts of the plant are poisonous or toxic (rhizome and leaves); if mistakenly ingested, it can cause stomach pains and vomiting. Also handling the plant may cause a skin irritation or an allergic reaction.<ref name=daves/><ref name=botanical/>
